source: CAPS FET Mathematics Gr 10-12, s.3.2.3 Topic allocation per term

objectives.objective: Number patterns, including arithmetic and geometric sequences and series
Sigma notation
Derivation and application of the formulae for the sum of arithmetic and geometric series (the three formulae listed as 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 are lost in the source extraction)
Definition of a function
General concept of the inverse of a function and how the domain of the function may need to be restricted (in order to obtain a one-to-one function) to ensure that the inverse is a function
Determine and sketch graphs of the inverses of the functions defined by the listed function forms (the defining equations are lost in the source extraction)

Focus on the following characteristics of the inverse graphs: domain and range, intercepts with the axes, turning points, minima, maxima, asymptotes (horizontal and vertical), shape and symmetry, average gradient (average rate of change), intervals on which the function increases/decreases

Revision of the exponential function and the exponential laws and graph of the function defined by an exponential equation with conditions on the base (the equation and its conditions are lost in the source extraction)
Understand the definition of a logarithm (the defining statement and its conditions are lost in the source extraction)
The graph of the function defined by y = log_b x for both the cases 0 < b < 1 and b > 1
Solve problems involving present value and future value annuities
Make use of logarithms to calculate the value of n, the time period, in the equations A = P(1 + i)ⁿ or a second compound growth/decay equation (lost in the source extraction)
Critically analyse investment and loan options and make informed decisions as to best option(s) (including pyramid)
Compound angle identities (the list of identities is lost in the source extraction)
Solve problems in two and three dimensions
Factorise third-degree polynomials. Apply the Remainder and Factor Theorems to polynomials of degree at most 3 (no proofs required)
An intuitive understanding of the limit concept, in the context of approximating the rate of change or gradient of a function at a point

Use limits to define the derivative of a function f at any x (limit formula lost in the source extraction). Generalise to find the derivative of f at any point x in the domain of f, i.e., define the derivative function f'(x) of the function f(x)
Understand intuitively that f'(a) is the gradient of the tangent to the graph of f at the point with x-coordinate a
Using the definition (first principle), find the derivative, f'(x) for a, b and c constants, of the listed functions (3.1 and 3.2 lost in the source extraction); f(x) = a/x; and f(x) = c
Use the formula for the derivative of xⁿ (for any real number n) together with the rules 4.1 (sum rule) and 4.2 (k a constant); the formulae themselves are lost in the source extraction
Find equations of tangents to graphs of functions
Introduce the second derivative of f(x) and how it determines the concavity of a function

Sketch graphs of cubic polynomial functions using differentiation to determine the co-ordinate of stationary points, and points of inflection (where concavity changes). Also, determine the x-intercepts of the graph using the factor theorem and other techniques
Solve practical problems concerning optimisation and rate of change, including calculus of motion
The equation of a circle with radius r and centre (a; b) (the equation itself is lost in the source extraction)
Determination of the equation of a tangent to a given circle
Revise earlier work on the necessary and sufficient conditions for polygons to be similar

Prove (accepting results established in earlier grades) that a line drawn parallel to one side of a triangle divides the other two sides proportionally (and the Mid-point Theorem as a special case of this theorem)
Prove (accepting results established in earlier grades) that equiangular triangles are similar
Prove (accepting results established in earlier grades) that triangles with sides in proportion are similar
Prove (accepting results established in earlier grades) the Pythagorean Theorem by similar triangles
Revise symmetric and skewed data

Use statistical summaries, scatterplots, regression (in particular the least squares regression line) and correlation to analyse and make meaningful comments on the context associated with given bivariate data, including interpolation, extrapolation and discussions on skewness
Revise dependent and independent events
Revise the product rule for independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
Revise the sum rule for mutually exclusive events A and B: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Revise the identity for P(A or B) in terms of P(A), P(B) and P(A and B) (formula partly lost in the source extraction)
Revise the complementary rule for P(not A) (formula partly lost in the source extraction)

Probability problems using Venn diagrams, trees, two-way contingency tables and other techniques (like the fundamental counting principle) to solve probability problems (where events are not necessarily independent)
Apply the fundamental counting principle to solve probability problems
